text: Smokers with COPD showed increased neutrophils and CD8+ cells within airway smooth muscle compared with non-smokers, suggesting these cells may drive smoking-induced airflow limitation. Investigators examined surgical specimens from 26 thoracotomy subjects—eight smokers with COPD, ten smokers with normal lung function, and eight non-smoking controls—using immunohistochemistry to quantify neutrophils, macrophages, mast cells, and CD4+/CD8+ cells in peripheral airway smooth muscle. Smokers with normal lung function also had neutrophilic infiltration, but to a lesser extent. Across all subjects, neutrophilic infiltration was inversely related to forced expiratory volume in 1 second (% predicted). COPD is an inflammatory disorder of chronic airflow limitation whose link to functional abnormalities remains uncertain, and inflammatory cell–smooth muscle interaction may be crucial. The microlocalisation of neutrophils and CD8+ cells implicates them in the pathogenesis of smoking-induced airflow limitation.
